origin_region: West Bengal · Dooars and Terai plains (Jalpaiguri, Alipurduar, Siliguri)
cultivar: Assam-type seedling bushes and Tocklai clones
processing: Mostly CTC, with a minority of orthodox factories; fully oxidised black tea from the lowland foothill plains below Darjeeling and Bhutan.
harvest_season: March to November; the summer and monsoon crop is the bulk, while spring teas are lighter and a little more aromatic.
appearance_dry: Dark granules or, for orthodox lots, twisted black leaf with little tip.
taste_profile: Mid-weight and smooth: lightly malty, mildly sweet, less punchy than Assam and without Darjeeling's florals.

brewing.notes: Takes milk; orthodox lots can be brewed a second time.

vintage_note: Sold year-round through the Siliguri and Kolkata auctions and mostly blended into Indian packet tea and tea bags; it is the backbone of many 'Darjeeling-style' and breakfast blends and is used to stretch dearer teas. Rarely sold by estate abroad; when it is, the lot carries the garden and the season rather than any vintage.
description:
The Dooars and the Terai are the flat, wet foothill plains at the base of the Himalayas in northern West Bengal: the Terai around Siliguri just below Darjeeling, and the Dooars stretching east along the Bhutan border. Together they make far more tea than Darjeeling, almost all of it plain black tea for the Indian market, and most of it never carries a place name at all.

The gardens grow Assam-type bushes and most factories make CTC, though a minority make orthodox leaf. Manufacture is conventional: wither, cut or roll, full oxidation and firing, with grades sorted by size. The bulk of the crop comes in the summer and monsoon months; spring teas are lighter and a little more aromatic.

The cup is mid-weight and smooth, lightly malty and mildly sweet, without the punch of Assam or the fragrance of the hills. It takes milk well and suits a long steep with water near the boil; orthodox lots can be brewed twice.

It is sold year-round through the Siliguri and Kolkata auctions and blended into Indian packet tea and tea bags, where it is often the backbone of 'Darjeeling-style' and breakfast blends; the trade also uses Dooars leaf to stretch more expensive teas. Single-garden lots are rare abroad, and when they appear they carry the garden name and season rather than any vintage.

Worth knowing about mostly so that you understand what is inside a cheap 'Darjeeling blend', and because an honest Dooars orthodox is good value for a daily milk tea.
sources_note: Native name in Bengali for the Dooars only. No dedicated tea article on Wikipedia; the regional article is used as umbrella.
